papers.title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
papers.how_tested: LLM agents in repeated Cournot markets under ungoverned, prompt-constitution, and governance-graph regimes; the governance graph includes warning/fine/suspension states with time-expiry edges and a compliance-credit path back to Active (restorative re-entry), bundled into the Institutional regime rather than ablated.
papers.finding: The Institutional regime cut severe collusion from 50% to 5.6% across six model configurations (N=90), but the restorative path's separate contribution is not isolated.

papers.title: Competition and Cooperation of LLM Agents in Games
papers.how_tested: LLM agents play network resource-allocation and Cournot games; in one controlled perturbation the environment injects an opponent defection and then an opponent quantity reduction (labelled an 'apology'), and the LLM agent's fitted trust/inequity-aversion parameters are tracked.
papers.finding: The LLM agent retaliated tit-for-tat after the injected betrayal and returned to cooperation after the injected concession, i.e. it 'forgave'; this is a single illustrative trajectory with a scripted, behavioural (not verbal) apology.

papers.title: Cultural Evolution of Cooperation among LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: Generations of LLM agents play an iterated donation game (give to a recipient who cannot directly repay), conditioning on recipients' behavioural traces; cooperation norms evolve culturally across base models.
papers.finding: Evolution of cooperation differed sharply across base models, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet societies reaching higher scores than Gemini 1.5 Flash and GPT-4o; the mechanism is downstream indirect reciprocity (reputation), not upstream/generalised reciprocity, so it is only partial evidence for a gift economy.

papers.title: Static network structure cannot stabilize cooperation among large language model agents
papers.how_tested: LLM agents (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Mixtral) play repeated Prisoner's Dilemma in well-mixed populations vs fixed ring networks, varying degree k and benefit-to-cost ratio, benchmarked against human network experiments.
papers.finding: Unlike humans, LLMs cooperated more in well-mixed populations and did not adjust to fixed network ties, so stable embedding did not stabilize cooperation.

papers.title: NetworkGames: Simulating Cooperation in Network Games with Personality-driven LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: MBTI-persona LLM agents play the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma on small-world and scale-free networks of different sizes and across several LLMs, varying where personality types sit in the network.
papers.finding: Network connectivity and the placement of personalities jointly determined cooperation: small-world networks inhibited it and prosocial agents at scale-free hubs raised it. This is partial evidence, since it covers network topology rather than social capital or trust.

papers.title: Gifting in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (Student Abstract)
papers.how_tested: Independent RL agents in a resource-appropriation (commons) setting are given an extra action to deliberately pass reward to other agents.
papers.finding: Reward gifting greatly improved learning progression in the resource appropriation setting; preliminary analysis of its effect on learning dynamics.

papers.title: Emergent Prosociality in Multi-Agent Games Through Gifting
papers.how_tested: Self-interested learning agents in multi-equilibrium (high-risk coordination) games may transfer part of their reward to peers; analysed with dynamical-systems theory and simulations.
papers.finding: Gifting enlarged the basins of attraction of prosocial equilibria and substantially improved convergence to them without external reward shaping.

papers.title: The Role of Network Topology and Opponent Information in Shaping Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems
papers.how_tested: Deep RL agents placed as nodes of graphs play iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with neighbours; network topology and the opponent information available (action history, identity) are manipulated.
papers.finding: Neighbours per node and average path length were the main drivers of emergent cooperation; opponent identity information reduced cooperative strategy adoption.

papers.title: Learning to Participate through Trading of Reward Shares
papers.how_tested: Independently trained RL agents in general-sum Markov games / social dilemmas can buy equity-like shares in other agents' rewards (stock-market-inspired mechanism).
papers.finding: Holding shares in others' returns led agents to cooperate and, in extended domains, to specialize and divide subtasks. This is partial evidence: tradable reward shares are only an analogue of worker-cooperative ownership.

notes: (1) Primitives 10, 11 and 17 are mostly true gaps: only P17-03 (network embeddedness) has direct LLM tests (han2025static). Everything else is partial or untested. (2) Partial calls to check: yao2026competition's 'apology' is a scripted opponent concession in one illustrative trajectory. The restorative path in bracalesyrnikov2026institutional is bundled with sanctions, so there is no causal isolation. vallinder2024cultural is indirect reciprocity (arguably belongs to the reputation primitive). The MARL gifting papers may belong more naturally to a peer-reward/incentive primitive. (3) Excluded but adjacent: 'Why Do Language Model Agents Whistleblow?' (arXiv 2511.17085; single agent, to external parties); 'Training Agents to Self-Report Misbehavior' (arXiv 2602.22303; single agent, self-incrimination); 'Mapping Human Anti-collusion Mechanisms to Multi-agent AI Systems' (arXiv 2601.00360; conceptual only, counts as discussed for P10-01); Leng & Yuan 'Do LLM Agents Exhibit Social Behavior?' (arXiv 2312.15198; upstream/downstream reciprocity, but one LLM against simulated partners); 'The challenge of hidden gifts in MARL' (arXiv 2505.20579; unobserved beneficial acts, a credit-assignment framing, possible weak P17-02 MARL evidence); Ueshima et al. 2023 ostracism MARL (arXiv 2310.04623; exclusion without reintegration, fits a separate exclusion primitive); 'From Certain Doom to Survival' (arXiv 2609.22600; LLM-authored governance with redistribution and exile, abstract only, not checked for restorative content). (4) SanctSim, named in the seed notes, could not be found by web search; the verifier should confirm its identity. (5) Some papers are 2026 preprints (2601.11369, 2604.00487, 2608.28977); titles and years are from their arXiv abs pages.
